course.title: Principles of Microeconomics
course.description: How individuals, firms, and markets make decisions under scarcity — supply, demand, elasticity, costs, and competition. Structure adapted from OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 2e (CC BY 4.0).

lessons.title: Scarcity, choice, and opportunity cost
lessons.grammar_note: Opportunity cost = the next-best thing you gave up, not the dollar price.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain scarcity and compute opportunity cost. Warm-up: in one sentence, what does economics study?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Resources are *scarce* — limited relative to wants — so every choice trades off against another. The *opportunity cost* of a choice is the value of the best alternative you didn't pick. The *production possibilities frontier* (PPF) shows the maximum of two goods an economy can make; points inside are inefficient, points outside are unreachable.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: You have one free evening. Studying earns a better grade; a concert earns fun. If you study, the opportunity cost is the concert — not $0, even though studying is 'free'. On a PPF of guns vs butter, making more guns costs some butter.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: You spend $12 and 2 hours on a movie you could have used to earn $15 tutoring. Opportunity cost? Answer: the $15 (plus the enjoyment) of tutoring — the best forgone alternative. Which PPF point is wasteful: inside or outside? Answer: inside.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: counting only money and ignoring time/forgone options. Mistake: thinking 'free' means zero opportunity cost. Exit: (a) Define opportunity cost. (b) A point outside the PPF is…? Answers: best alternative forgone; currently unattainable.

lessons.title: Demand
lessons.grammar_note: Movement ALONG a curve = price change; SHIFT of the curve = something else.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State the law of demand and tell a shift from a movement. Warm-up: when price rises, quantity demanded does what?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The *law of demand*: as price rises, quantity demanded falls (all else equal). A *change in price* moves you along the demand curve. A *change in a determinant* — income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, number of buyers — *shifts* the whole curve.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Coffee price jumps: quantity demanded falls — a movement along the curve. Now a study says coffee boosts health: at every price people want more — the curve shifts right.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Shift or movement? (1) Tea (a substitute) gets cheaper, affecting coffee. (2) Coffee's own price falls. Answers: (1) shift left (people buy tea instead), (2) movement along.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling a price-driven change a 'shift'. Exit: (a) Name two demand shifters. (b) A price change causes a ___ along the curve. Answers: e.g. income, tastes; movement.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Find equilibrium and predict shortages/surpluses. Warm-up: at equilibrium, how do quantity supplied and demanded compare?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The *law of supply*: as price rises, quantity supplied rises. *Equilibrium* is the price where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded — the market clears. Above it, a *surplus* pushes price down; below it, a *shortage* pushes price up.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: If demand is 100 at $5 and supply is 100 at $5, $5 is equilibrium. Set price at $7 (above): suppliers offer 130 but buyers want 70 → surplus of 60 → price falls back toward $5.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: At $3, demand 120, supply 80. Shortage or surplus, and which way does price move? Answer: shortage of 40; price rises. A rise in input costs shifts supply which way? Answer: left (up).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking price 'sets' quantity — both curves do together. Exit: (a) A surplus does what to price? (b) Supply shifts left when input costs…? Answers: lowers it; rise.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compute price elasticity and read it. Warm-up: if quantity barely changes when price rises, is demand elastic or inelastic?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Price elasticity of demand* = (% change in quantity) ÷ (% change in price), in absolute value. Greater than 1 = *elastic* (responsive); less than 1 = *inelastic*; equal to 1 = *unit elastic*. Necessities and addictive goods tend to be inelastic; luxuries with substitutes are elastic.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Price up 10%, quantity down 25% → elasticity = 25/10 = 2.5 → elastic. Price up 20%, quantity down 5% → 5/20 = 0.25 → inelastic (think insulin).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Price +10%, Q −4%: elastic or inelastic, value? Answer: 0.4, inelastic. If a firm raises price and total revenue rises, is demand elastic or inelastic? Answer: inelastic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting elasticity uses percentages, not raw units. Exit: (a) Elasticity of 3 means…? (b) Necessities are usually…? Answers: elastic/very responsive; inelastic.

lessons.title: Costs of production and competition
lessons.grammar_note: Profit-max rule: produce where marginal revenue = marginal cost.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Separate fixed from variable costs and state how a competitive firm chooses output. Warm-up: is rent a fixed or variable cost?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Fixed costs* don't vary with output (rent); *variable costs* do (materials). *Marginal cost* is the cost of one more unit. In *perfect competition* — many firms, identical product, free entry — firms are *price takers* and produce where *marginal revenue = marginal cost*. Free entry pushes long-run economic profit toward zero.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A bakery pays $100 rent (fixed) and $2 per loaf (variable). At a market price of $3, each loaf adds $3 revenue and $2 cost → make more until MC rises to $3.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify: (1) machine lease, (2) flour, (3) hourly wages. Answers: 1 fixed, 2 variable, 3 variable. A price-taking firm produces where MR = ? Answer: MC.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: including sunk fixed costs in the produce-one-more decision (only marginal cost matters there). Exit: (a) Competitive firms set output where MR = ? (b) Long-run competitive profit trends toward…? Answers: MC; zero.

lessons.title: Applied project: price a real product

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Pick a real product you could sell (a service, a craft, a resold item). Use the course tools to reason about its price — you're building an argument, not a spreadsheet.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) State the product and your fixed and variable costs. 2) Judge whether demand is likely elastic or inelastic and why (substitutes? necessity?). 3) Name one thing that would shift demand right. 4) Propose a price and justify it with marginal reasoning (would one more sale add more revenue than cost?).

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ Costs correctly split into fixed vs variable. ✔ Elasticity judgment has a stated reason. ✔ A demand shifter (not a price change) is identified. ✔ The price is justified by marginal revenue vs marginal cost, not gut feel. Four checks = you've priced like an economist.
